title: From model to code
text: Even without generation, models are useful: to communicate, to analyse, to validate a design before it is built. They start to drive development when a program reads them and systematically derives something from them: code, other models, tests, documentation. That program is a generator.

title: What a generator does
text: Start with the problem. In a typical business application, the same data structure turns up again and again: as a database table, as a server class, as a transfer object, as a model in the browser, as a form. Writing these by hand is tedious and error-prone — and it is schematic : knowing the data structure, you could almost type the rest blindfolded. That is exactly what can be generated. Most generators work like mail merge. A letter template has placeholders, and a list of addresses fills them, one letter per address. A code template is the target code with holes in it, and the model fills the holes: The model carries the domain , the templates carry the technology : swap the templates — and the runtime parts they rely on — and the same model can produce code for another platform. And one model line reaches every tier at once. Try it — add attributes to Book : You may have used generators like this. Prisma derives database tables and a typed client from one schema file; OpenAPI Generator turns one API description into clients, servers and documentation. The generators in this article work the same way, with one difference that matters: they are not run once to get started, but again and again, with every change to the model. A real generator does more than fill templates. It reads the model and checks it, transforms it into a structure closer to the target — adding, for example, an id nobody modelled — and only then generates . Step inside: And a generator adds things that were never in the model at all — login, the wiring of the database — on top of a hand-built runtime environment , the ready-made part the generated code plugs into [8] . Code generation is the process of translating a source model into artifacts of an executable language. [2] Inside real generators Why an intermediate tree. When the input and the output language are far apart, it pays to transform the input’s AST into one that fits the output first. One model, several meanings. The same model can be mapped differently: a state Off might become an enum constant, an integer, a subclass or a method. So the meaning has to be settled before a generator is built. Configurable generators. Templates can be replaced at hook points, and generators should be able to leave out what a project does not use — unused generated endpoints are a security issue [BGK+24] . MontiCore, the tool that builds the tools Where do the languages CD4A, GUI-DSL and OCL/P come from, with their parsers, symbol tables and checks? From MontiCore, a language workbench developed at RWTH Aachen since 2004 [9] . MontiCore builds the tools that read your models: from a grammar it generates the parser, the tree classes, the symbol table and the frame for the rule checks; the language engineer adds the rules, the tool builder the transformations and templates. Its strength is composition: languages are built from languages — the GUI-DSL refers to CD4A through symbols, OCL/P embeds an expression language. That is how MontiGem’s family of languages could grow without being rewritten. MontiCore handbook (PDF) ↗ the reference, free monticore.github.io ↗ documentation, the languages CD4A and OCL

title: Generated and hand-written code
text: Complete generation is rare: real systems mix generated and hand-written code — the business rule no model covers, the special screen, the connection to an old system. The rule that makes this work is simple: never edit generated code . The next generation run overwrites it. A one-off scaffold is still a useful start — but only a generator that can be run again keeps helping a system whose models keep changing [DGM+21] . Instead, hand-written code builds on the generated code. MontiCore and MontiGem use the TOP mechanism for this: if a hand-written class Loan exists, the generator names its own class LoanTOP , and the hand-written class extends it. Everything else in the system keeps using the name Loan and gets the hand-written version. The price is small but real: the generator has to look for hand-written files, so after adding or removing one you regenerate once. And the trick has a limit: page models are trees, not classes, so there is nothing to extend — how pages are customised instead is shown under CD2GUI . The lesson from five projects is plain: a code generator has to support hand-written extensions [BGK+24] . Generation Gap and other mechanisms The general pattern. TOP is a variant of the Generation Gap pattern: “separate generated code from non-generated code by inheritance”, first described by John Vlissides [10] . C# partial classes solve the same problem without inheritance. Other mechanisms. Delegation, or “protected regions” inside generated files that the generator leaves alone — the last are fragile [11] . Separate folders. Hand-written and generated code live in separate directory trees. Many projects keep generated code out of version control and regenerate it in every build; others check it in to review what the generator changed — a choice of workflow, not a law. Not round-trip engineering. Code is never fed back into the model: the model stays the source, the code is always derived.

Right, the TOP mechanism: when a hand-written class Loan exists, the generator emits LoanTOP instead, and Loan extends it. The price: after adding a hand-written file you regenerate once. EDIT THE GENERATED CODE out/Loan.java // generated — do not edit public class Loan { Date due; Date getDue() {…} } The generator writes Loan.java. EXTEND IT (TOP MECHANISM) out/Loan.java // generated — do not edit public class Loan { Date due; Date getDue() {…} } Same start. After [7] , Fig. 14.5

title: When the model changes
text: Regenerating is safe for the code . But a running system also has data , and that data was stored in the shape of the old model. When the model changes, the code is simply regenerated, but the data already stored may have to be converted: Database tools draw the same line: Prisma generates a migration for the new structure, and filling the new columns from the old ones is a step you write into that migration yourself. So plan models for growth: additions are usually easier to absorb than changes to what is already there — though even a new attribute needs a migration when the records already stored must have a value for it. Model evolution in practice and research Practice confirms the rule of thumb: in MaCoCo, additions to the models took less time than changes, which also touched hand-written code and, in the data model, required data migrations in the running application [DGM+21] . Research goes one step further: comparing two versions of a model not line by line but by meaning — what can the new model express that the old one could not? That is what my work on the evolution of domain models looks at [BNR+25] .

title: Whole applications from one model
text: Model-driven techniques are used far beyond business software — in embedded and cyber-physical systems, software product lines, system analysis. From here on, this article stays with data-centric web applications, where the ideas show most clearly, and with one toolchain, MontiCore and MontiGem. The pieces come together: a generator that turns a class diagram into a web application, a language for its pages, a transformation that derives the pages by itself — and what all of this has to do with low-code and AI. The chapter ends with a case study from practice and what the approach costs.

title: Why business applications repeat themselves
text: Think of the software that administrations run on: finances, staff, inventory, loans. Lists, forms and detail pages over a central database — and at their core always the same four operations: create, read, update and delete, CRUD for short. Such information systems are big, but their structure repeats with every class of the data model. You have probably seen this used: Django’s admin reads the models of an application and builds management pages from them, though it is meant as an internal tool, not as the application itself; Rails’ scaffold generator writes model, controller, views and a database migration for a resource in one command — once, as a starting point to edit by hand. MontiGem — the MontiCore-based Generator for Enterprise Management — goes the whole way. The class diagram is the only mandatory model [GMN+20] ; page models, rules and access tags can be added. From them it generates a complete, data-centric three-tier application — a database with its access layer, a Java server, an Angular/TypeScript front end — and it keeps regenerating it as the models change, with hand-written code kept apart as above. Because all tiers come from one model, their interfaces fit together by construction. What a class diagram does not say — business rules, workflows, connections to other systems — is added through further models or hand-written extensions. This is a whole page model, slightly simplified — in MaCoCo, a page usually gets its data through a separate view-model class: webpage Books(all Book b) { card { head { label "Books" } body { datatable { rows <b { column "Title", title column "Pages", pages }}}}} all Book b loads all books; rows <b makes one table row per book; column "Title", title shows the attribute title from the class diagram. Data, page and rules, each in its own language, end up on one screen: One piece of advice from practice: do not bury large amounts of hand-written HTML inside page models — they become as hard to read as the HTML itself; keep highly specific parts entirely hand-written [BGK+24] .

title: CD2GUI: from a class diagram to an application
text: Page models still have to be written. CD2GUI removes even that step: from one class diagram it derives the page models by itself. Its output is not code but more models — a model-to-model transformation — which MontiGem then turns into code as if someone had written them by hand. For every class there is an overview page (all objects in a table) and a details page (one object with its attributes and associations), plus one dashboard for all classes [GMN+20] . A model transformation applies to one or more source models and transforms them into one or more target models. [2] And when the library wants something else on the member page — two buttons, for a new loan and a reminder? Not in the generated HTML: in a small hand-written delta model with operations such as remove , replace , add_to , add_before and add_after , applied to the generated page tree before code is generated. That is the answer to TOP’s limit: since the change lives in a model, it survives every regeneration. Which components the pages get is decided by simple rules: The concept appeared in 2020; its first use in a real project was the digital-twin cockpits for wind turbines [MNN+22] — see the ADD project . title: When requirements change: titles and copies
text: A generated application is a start, not the end. Say the library finds that Book mixes two things: the title in the catalogue and the physical copies on the shelf. Copies must be tracked one by one, and no copy may be lent twice at the same time. The model changes — available moves to a new class BookCopy , and a loan now points to a copy: classdiagram Library { class Book { String title; int pages; } class BookCopy { boolean available; } class Member { String name; } class Loan { Date due; } association [1] Book -> (copies) BookCopy [*]; association [1] Member -> (loans) Loan [*]; association [*] Loan -> (copy) BookCopy [1]; } Regenerating brings the tables, server classes and transfer objects for copies and, through CD2GUI, their overview and details pages, with each book’s copies on its details page. Three things it does not bring. The rule “one open loan per copy” is not in a class diagram: it needs an OCL/P invariant or a hand-written check — and a way to tell open loans from returned ones, which the model does not have yet. The lending workflow — check out, return, remind — is hand-written code or further models on top of the generated pages. And the loans already stored point to books, not copies: a migration has to create the copies and re-link the loans. Nothing is thrown away, though: the application is regenerated around the new model, and only the hand-written parts that touched a book’s availability need adapting.

title: Where this leads: low-code and AI
text: Low-code platforms promise applications without programming. Seen from MDE, many of them are a familiar recipe: a modelling language behind the wizards, plus ready-made building blocks and a platform that runs the result — even when the language is never named [12] . The form designer is a page model, the data source is a class diagram. Platforms differ in what they do with the models: some generate code, as MontiGem does; others interpret the models while the application runs. Both are model-driven. Will business people now write their software themselves? The same was promised for COBOL [6] , and low-code languages tend to grow back into fuller languages over time. The realistic role for citizen developers is that of co-authors of models — which is what this article is meant to prepare for. And then there is AI. Writing the model is the step that still takes expertise — and it is the one an LLM can help with: describe the domain in a sentence, the LLM writes the class diagram, and CD2GUI and MontiGem do the rest, deterministically. In our 2024 experiments, GPT-4 asked for a CD4A model without any context wrote no valid one in 20 tries. A predefined conversation that explained the key rules of the language raised this to 99 of 100 for one task; giving examples instead reached 88 of 100 [NMR24] . “Valid” means the CD4A parser accepted the model — whether it describes the right domain is a separate question that the parser cannot answer; it stays with the domain expert. How an LLM works, how it learns a modelling language and how a grammar keeps it from writing invalid models is the subject of part 2 of this series: AI-driven software engineering — continue with language models that write models .

title: Case study: MaCoCo and four other domains
text: MontiGem did not start on a whiteboard but in a running system. MaCoCo , the management cockpit RWTH chairs use for their finances, staff and projects, began as a hand-written application; generation was added to it one aspect at a time, following a method of 16 activities [DGM+21] . MaCoCo in numbers [GLM+24] — code and models as of March 2022, users at the time of the report: 74.59 % of the implementation code generated 500,573 generated lines 73 · 74 domain classes · GUI models 1,403 users at 188 chairs and institutes The share compares lines of code: 500,573 generated against 170,505 hand-written; the 14,251 lines of models are not counted (with them, it would be about 73 %). It measures how much of the code is generated — not how much effort was saved. And it is not “generated instead of hand-written”: every page consists of generated base code that is extended and optimised by hand. After about three years, the generator was extracted from MaCoCo into a framework of its own, MontiGem, and used in four more domains [BGK+24] : tool tracking for craftsmen with Ford , energy management of buildings, the privacy policies of wearables (InviDas), and the engineering of wind turbines ( ADD ). What the five projects taught is summed up below, under what it costs and when this approach pays off ; more on the MontiGem project page .

title: What it costs
text: None of this comes free. The costs are engineering trade-offs, and the five MontiGem projects show where they lie [BGK+24] : An investment up front. Languages, generators, templates and the runtime environment have to be built before they pay off — which is why reusing them across projects matters. Retrofitting a generator into a running system is harder still, but paid off in the long run. Two things to maintain. Models and generator evolve together: every project brought new patterns that had to go into the tooling. Debugging across layers. An error can sit in the model, a transformation, a template, the generated code or the runtime. In the projects this stayed manageable as long as the mapping from model to code was straightforward. Extension boundaries. Generated parts have to be replaceable where they meet existing systems, and very specific screens are better written entirely by hand. Expertise. Someone has to model well and someone has to maintain the languages; all five projects had MDE experts on board.

title: In short
text: A model is a purposeful simplification of an original: ask what it is for, not whether it is complete. The picture is not the model: behind text and diagram sits a structure that tools can check (in MontiCore, a tree) — and “it parses” is not “it is correct”. A DSL gives up generality to get close to one domain; you already use several. A generator works like mail merge for code and carries architectural decisions: one model line becomes consistent code in every tier. Generated and hand-written code are kept apart , so you can regenerate at any time — the value lies in repeated generation, not in a one-shot scaffold. CD2GUI and MontiGem turn one class diagram into a running, data-centric prototype that grows into a full-size system without being thrown away. Many low-code platforms are MDE with a platform and a friendlier surface; AI fits in front of it: the LLM writes only the model, and a deterministic, testable generator does the rest. The central benefit is not that models can generate code. It is that domain decisions stay explicit, checkable and reusable for the whole life of a system: when models, generators and hand-written extensions evolve together, a first prototype can grow into a full-size application without abandoning its models. title: / 4 Digital Twins
text: article · 2026 What a digital twin is — and what it is not: models, digital shadows and services, how a twin acts, and how to build twins with models. Series 1 Model-driven engineering 2 AI in software engineering 3 Digital twins 4 Evolutionary algorithms Interactive figures require JavaScript. Static diagrams, captions and source tables remain available; displayed demo values are illustrative unless labeled as publication data. Your electric car’s app shows its charge level and range, live, wherever you are. Is that a digital twin? Many would say yes. By the end of the first chapter you will be able to say why that alone is insufficient under the definition used here — and what is missing. “Digital twin” has become one of the most used and least agreed-on words in engineering. This article uses the definition of the Software Engineering group at RWTH Aachen and the Internet of Production, a large research cluster at RWTH Aachen on digital production [1] . It builds on part 1 of this series: a twin is software , made of models , and it can be engineered with generators . Chapter 01 explains the concepts on a car. Chapter 02 shows how a twin works on the case study of the RWTH group’s papers, the injection-moulding machine in the figure above. Chapter 03 builds twins with models, with wind turbines as a second case study.

title: What a digital twin is
text: The example for this chapter is something you know: a car. First the why, then three words that are often confused — model, shadow, twin — the definition, and the difference between the twin of a car model and the twin of your car.

title: Systems that outlive their software
text: Production machines run for ten to fifteen years, bridges for fifty, buildings for up to a hundred. Over that time they are watched, maintained, adjusted and extended — and the knowledge needed for this is scattered across drawings, sensor logs and people’s heads. The software that watches over such a structure ages much faster than the structure itself [2] . A digital twin brings that knowledge together and puts it to work: monitoring what happens, predicting what will happen, simulating what would happen, assisting the people who operate the system and, in the end, controlling it. The precondition is an identifiable original system whose relevant states or events can be observed and, where appropriate, influenced. Physical assets are common examples, but the definition also permits workflows and software systems [5] .

title: Systems that outlive their software.
text: Systems that outlive their software. Grey: how long the original system lives. Accent: software support periods of 10 years — as long as Microsoft supported Windows 10 [3] . These repeated Windows 10-length windows illustrate maintenance planning, not a measured generic software lifetime. A twin may need continuity across several such generations. Estimates of the lifespans vary between sources. After [4] , p. 2

title: Model, shadow, twin: the data-flow view
text: The most popular way to tell the three words apart comes from Kritzinger and colleagues [6] . It asks a single question: how automatically does data flow between the real system and its digital counterpart? A digital model has no automated data flow — the CAD model of your car. A digital shadow receives data automatically — the charge level in your app. A digital twin also sends data back automatically — say, a new charging limit, computed from the battery data and sent to the car without anyone typing it in. So the app is a shadow. The ladder is a good first step, but it has two limits. It says nothing about what a twin consists of [8] . And it disagrees with the definition used here about one case: if a person carries out what the twin proposes, Kritzinger calls it a shadow. Under RWTH, human-mediated control can count, provided models, regularly updated shadows and appropriate services are also present. Human involvement alone does not establish a twin.

title: Three words on one axis: how automatically does data flow?
section: Model, shadow, twin: the data-flow view
text: Three words on one axis: how automatically does data flow? A model is updated by hand, a shadow follows the system automatically, a twin also acts back on it. The ladder is intuitive — but it says nothing about what is inside the box, and it disagrees with the RWTH definition as soon as a person sits in the loop. What is inside the box → the next figure. DATA FLOW: digital shadow Data flows automatically from the car to the digital object. Example: the app on your phone shows charge level and range, live — but nothing in it changes the car by itself. example: ours After [6] · levels as described in [8]

title: The definition: what a twin consists of
text: The RWTH definition does not ask about data flow first, but about the parts. This article uses version 2.2 (2024): A digital twin of an original system is a software that consists of a set of models of the system and a set of digital shadows, both of which are purposefully updated on a regular basis, and provides a set of services to use both purposefully with respect to the original system. The digital twin interacts with the original system by providing useful information about the system’s context and sending it control commands. Rumpe, Michael, Wortmann [1] This component-and-interaction definition describes an operational twin . The same research calls coherent engineering artifacts created before the original exists a development twin , a separate lifecycle notion that need not yet have live shadows or commands. Read the operational clauses one by one. A twin is a software — not a 3D picture, not a single model. It contains models , because data alone means little: a structure model tells where each sensor sits, and so what its readings are about. It contains digital shadows — purpose-bound collections of data (below). Both are purposefully updated on a regular basis : at cadences appropriate to their purpose. Shadows may follow sensor events in seconds; engineering models may change after a repair or redesign. Identity, timestamps and synchronization policies connect these different cadences. Its services use them — monitoring, prediction, assistance, control. And it interacts with the original system in both directions: it informs, and it commands — from configurations up to hard real-time commands. How do the ladder and the definition fit together? They use the same three words differently: THE LADDER model → shadow → twin are stages , ordered by how automatically data flows. THE RWTH DEFINITION models and shadows are parts of a twin. A shadow can exist on its own, like the app. An operational twin under this definition contains shadows. And a twin contains models but is not itself a model [10] — the way an application contains a class diagram without being one. Its models come from engineering models or are abstracted from the data, which is where chapter 03 picks up. Where the definition comes from The definition has a history. The first version (2020) came out of a survey among the Internet of Production’s 25 departments and 200 researchers [11] : “A digital twin of a system consists of a set of models of the system, a set of digital shadows and their aggregation and abstraction collected from a system, and a set of services that allow using the data and models purposefully with respect to the original system.” A shorter form of 2022 is the one my own papers use. Version 2.0 added the regular updates and the way back; 2.1 followed discussions in the model-driven engineering community at a Dagstuhl seminar; 2.2 (2024) adds “is a software”. For people, the RWTH group proposes the same definition under another name — a digital companion , because “twin” means something else in medicine [1] .

Everything the definition asks for: models and shadows, kept up to date for a purpose, services that use them, and a way back — information and commands. After [9] , Fig. 1 · layout; verdicts ours

title: Digital shadows: data under a purpose
text: Why define shadows at all? Because a complete digital copy of a car — let alone a factory — is out of reach, and not needed. The Internet of Production started from the hypothesis that a well-designed collection of digital shadows is more promising than a full-scale digital twin [12] — much like a navigation app, which combines abstracted live data from many phones with a map. A digital shadow includes a set of contextual data traces and/or their aggregation and abstraction collected concerning a system for a specific purpose with respect to the original system. SE@RWTH [5] The key word is purpose : shadows are created or selected for a specific purpose, which may overlap with others. A SQL view illustrates a purpose-specific projection, not the entire contextual shadow: identity, source, units, timestamps, latency and provenance also matter. It is about an asset (your car), collects data traces from sources — sensors, but also people typing in values — and uses a model to make sense of them. Then it answers a question. It never acts: a shadow follows the original system under one particular view; a twin follows it too, but may also change its behaviour [FHM+23] .

title: The same data, three shadows.
section: Digital shadows: data under a purpose
text: The same data, three shadows. Each purpose picks other rows and columns of the same raw data and condenses them differently: the latest value, a maximum, the last two readings against a threshold. None of them acts — a shadow answers a question; it can be compared to a view in a database [13] . The latest value, not a charging recommendation: trip length and battery condition are not modeled. title: One type, many instances
text: A twin can exist before its original system is built. While a car model is being designed, its development twin is a coherent set of development artefacts. It has the character of a type , because it may have many instances, and it has no data from a real car, except perhaps from simulations [1] . Once cars are built, each one can have its own instance twin — as manufactured, with its tolerances, and as driven, with its wear. If you write software: the type/instance analogy is useful, but lifecycle twins are not literally classes and objects. Does each purpose get its own twin? The RWTH group answers with a riddle: “Logically, there is only one digital twin. If there were several twins, they would not be twins but triplets or more” [1] . In software terms: one logical system, possibly deployed as several services — in the car, at the edge, in the cloud. Why there are 112 definitions A mapping study of 356 papers collected 112 different definitions [15] . Their weak spots fall into four kinds: ambiguous (they defer to another undefined term such as “virtual representation”), narrow (one domain or technology), underspecified (only the data flow, as in the ladder) and utopian (a complete copy of everything). Where they part ways, this article takes one side: Question The stance taken here Does data flow back? Yes — directly or through people. Some definitions only mirror the system. A complete copy? No — a twin is always an abstraction for purposes. Early definitions aimed at describing a product completely. Passive or active? Active: a twin is a running software system, not a data structure synchronised from outside. Before the product exists? Yes: the development twin. In practice, though, 266 of the 356 papers address the operation phase, and only 29 develop the twin together with the system [16] .

title: One type, many instances — like a class and its objects.
text: One type, many instances — like a class and its objects. The class/object comparison is an analogy, not an implementation requirement. During design there is no car yet, so the twin is a development twin of the car model, valid for every car built from it. When instance twins are provisioned, each can record its own history that takes in its tolerances and, on the road, its wear. Grieves and Vickers call the two the Digital Twin Prototype and the Digital Twin Instance [14] . Illustrative · VINs, tolerances and battery health invented

title: How a twin works
text: The case study of this chapter is the injection-moulding machine that runs through the RWTH group’s twin papers [17] : what does its twin keep, how does it decide, and where do people come in?

title: Meet the machine
text: An injection-moulding machine makes plastic parts — here, door handles. Plastic granules fall from the hopper into a heated barrel . A screw turns inside it: it melts the granules with the heat of the heater bands and its own friction, and pushes a measured amount of melt to the front. Then the screw moves forward like a piston and injects the melt into the closed mould . The part cools, the clamping unit opens the mould, the part is ejected — and the cycle starts again. The control cabinet and the user interface set temperatures, pressures and times for every phase. So the twin’s data are temperatures of the barrel zones, pressures and the verdict OK / not OK for each part; the rejection rate is the share of faulty parts. Too hot, and the material degrades; too cold or too little pressure, and the mould is not filled. Finding the right settings by trial and error takes time, consumes energy and produces waste [DHM+22] .

title: From data to command: the twin’s loop
text: A thermostat is the smallest loop: measure, compare with the setpoint, switch the heater. A twin’s loop is the same, but each step is a replaceable model. In the injection-moulding twin, four components run in a loop: the data processor collects data and prepares it into shadows, the evaluator notices a problem, the reasoner chooses a fix, the executor sends the command — over standard protocols such as MQTT, OPC UA or REST. The intelligence consists of three kinds of small models: an event says when to act, a goal what should become true, a case how to get there. For a supported machine interface, new cases can adapt behavior without changing the core loop; new protocols, sensors or actuators may still require code. [DHM+22] . If no case matches, the reasoner looks for a similar one and adapts it into a new case. The shadow in step 2 is a view like the ones on the car in chapter 01: the last two readings of one sensor, for one purpose. From one loop to many services Since then, the loop has grown into a richer architecture [18] :

title: The twin’s intelligence is a chain of small, editable models.
section: From data to command: the twin’s loop
text: The twin’s intelligence is a chain of small, editable models. An event model says when to act, a goal what should become true, a case how to get there. Switch to operator approves : the loop stops at the cockpit until someone releases the proposal — some users do not want automatic execution, for fear of stopping a whole production line because of a wrong setting [4] . The architecture stays the same; one step changes. title: From one loop to many services.
section: From data to command: the twin’s loop
text: From one loop to many services. Grey arrows: telemetry and data access; accent arrows: authorized commands back through the gateway. The dashed cockpit path permits operator approval. Safety interlocks and authorization remain required. The self-adaptive loop — a variant of the classic monitor–analyse–plan–execute loop of self-adaptive systems (MAPE-K) — proved too rigid on its own, so later twins combine it with process-aware services (for example, noticing that opening the clamping unit takes too long), an optimiser and a cockpit. After [18] , Fig. 5.2 · simplified

title: People in the loop: cockpits
text: Twins can guide people, not only machines. Informative services show what is going on; assistive services lead a person step by step — in a smart kitchen, from “a fillable utensil that can hold at least 3 liters” to “left of the stove, in the drawer cabinet, in the first drawer from below” [4] . And a twin can explain itself: instead of “h > 70”, it can say that the vehicle stopped because its battery was overheating [19] . All of this needs a user interface — the twin’s cockpit: A digital twin cockpit is the user interaction part (UI/GUI) of a digital twin. It provides the graphical user interface for visualizations of its data organized in digital shadows and models, and the interaction with services of the digital twin, and thus enabling humans to access, adapt and add information and monitor and partially control the physical system. Bano et al. [20] , Def. 2 A first cockpit for the injection-moulding machine showed pressure, temperature and status — and a button for a full machine stop [11] . Who may issue a command is an operational and technical design decision: authorization, interlocks, safe limits and audit logs must support it. in published use cases the operator decides, or picks from a reduced set of options. You saw the switch in the loop above — it changes one step, not the architecture. Process-aware cockpits A process-aware cockpit also knows the steps of a process and who performs each — machine, twin or person. Such cockpits can be synthesised from event logs; the approach was tried on a hospital data set with 25,463 events and 6,455 cases [20] . Note: a cockpit in this sense is not the same as the management cockpit MaCoCo from part 1 — same word, different thing.

title: Building twins with models
text: If a twin must preserve continuity across several software generations, it needs the same discipline as any long-lived software — and models are the way to get it.

title: A twin is software, so engineer it
text: Twins use models in two ways: models inside the twin describe the machine; models of the twin describe the twin’s own software — and those are the ones we generate code from. Today, twins are mostly designed and built ad hoc, piece by piece [FHM+23] . Yet much of what a twin needs already exists: AutomationML, CAD or STEP files, Modelica or SysML models. Generators then do for twins what part 1 showed for information systems: they can produce cockpit components, data schemas and adapter skeletons when transformation rules and integration contracts are specified — generated from a few lines that say which sensor port feeds which attribute [10] . Hand-written parts survive regeneration, as with the TOP mechanism . Language models can draft such models, too: in my dissertation, GPT-4 produced a valid class diagram for a “Digital Twin of a Hydraulic Press” in 19 of 20 runs [Net24] . More in part 2 .

title: Do not start from scratch.
section: A twin is software, so engineer it
text: Do not start from scratch. Much of what a twin needs to know already exists as engineering models. Transformation and mapping specifications can generate schemas, UI and adapter skeletons. Deployment still needs data sources, identity and unit mappings, authentication, configured connectors, handwritten services and validation; models alone do not supply live shadows. After [4] , Fig. 3.1 · simplified

title: A platform that builds twins
text: WordPress builds websites; a site owner then builds pages without writing code. The same split works for twins. Who configures twins in practice? Mostly domain experts without a software-engineering education — our 2022 study addressed a gap in low-code configuration of twin behavior for these users [DHM+22] . So we generated a low-code platform for twins: MontiGem builds the workshop, and the twin designer uses the workshop to build twins. Three roles share the work: Our 2022 comparison covered related technologies with different roles: Eclipse Ditto is an open-source twin framework, AWS IoT Greengrass an edge runtime ecosystem, Microsoft DTDL a modeling language, and Siemens MindSphere an industrial IoT offering. Our contribution focused on domain experts configuring behavior in a generated low-code environment. The comparison describes the assessed workflows at that time, not a current market-wide limitation. Our approach is one possible implementation, and one question stays open: one big twin, or many separate ones?

title: Two generators, three roles.
text: Two generators, three roles. First the platform is generated, then the platform produces twins — configured by people who do not write code, with small models that can even change while the twin runs. title: Case study: a development twin for wind turbines
text: Wind turbines are adapted to every site, and their engineering parameters move between many tools. In the ADD project they were exchanged as e-mail attachments or links to temporary cloud storage — changes did not propagate fast enough, and the tools could not read each other’s formats [MNN+22] . Our answer was a single source of truth, generated from models: the turbine’s functional model became a class diagram, and MontiGem with CD2GUI generated the cockpit from it. Is this a digital twin? The paper presents a development-oriented twin prototype : an engineering information backbone for the turbine type, like the design example in chapter 01. It demonstrated model-derived CRUD views and engineering-tool writeback, not operational telemetry shadows, adaptive runtime services or turbine control under the operational v2.2 criteria. Details are on the ADD project page .

title: Twins over decades
text: Composition. A car is made of a powertrain, the powertrain of a battery, and many cars form a fleet — twins should be composed the same way, which raises questions of integration, intellectual property, rights and roles [21] . Evolution. A twin that lives for decades needs a way back from operation into the next development cycle [22] — and its software will be rebuilt several times on the way, which is where models and generators pay off. AI in and around twins. Process mining and AI are services of a twin; and language models can write the models twins are built from ( part 2 ). Part-of composition alone does not make twins interoperable: identity, units, time bases, ownership and service contracts must align. Several views can share one logical twin; independently governed twins need explicit integration. A digital thread emphasizes lifecycle traceability, while a cyber-physical system combines computation with a physical process; neither term alone establishes the twin services described here.

title: Twins of twins.
text: Twins of twins. “When composing a car chassis with a motor, the corresponding digital twins should be composed as well” [FHM+23] — today they are mostly built one by one. A fleet twin goes one level up and aggregates the twins of many cars. Composing twins raises open questions: integration across levels, intellectual property, rights and roles. After [21] , Fig. 1 · redrawn for a car

title: In short
text: A twin is software made of models and digital shadows plus services, and it interacts with its original system — it is “not only a simulation model, it is not only a dashboard, and it is not just another term for a CPS” [4] . A shadow is passive and is selected for a purpose, with SQL projections as one implementation analogy; the twin also acts. Two views of three words: the ladder asks how automatically data flows; the RWTH definition asks what is inside — models and shadows are parts of a twin, not stages before it. Type and instance: development and operational twins describe different lifecycle perspectives; class/object is only an analogy. Humans stay in the loop: the cockpit is the twin’s interface, and whether a command runs automatically is a design decision. Engineer twins model-driven: continuity across software generations is a design goal. Models and generators help build components; integration and runtime validation remain engineering work. Lifecycle data may be archived after asset retirement. A TWIN IS WORTH IT WHEN there is an identifiable original system with relevant observable states or events the system lives long enough to repay the effort someone will act on what it says — automatically or through people A SHADOW MAY BE ENOUGH WHEN you only need to watch or analyse no twin service needs to initiate an intervention, even through a person there is no way to act back on the system TRY IT YOURSELF SysML v2 Model Creator ↗ model a system, e.g. a pump, in SysML v2 CD4A Class Diagram Creator ↗ its data as a class diagram MontiCore Expert ↗ MontiCore’s language components and handbook

title: / 4 Evolutionary Algorithms
text: article · 2026 Evolution as an algorithm: many guesses, a score, and a few rules for which guesses get to have children — what evolutionary algorithms are, how each step works, and when to use them. Series 1 Model-driven engineering 2 AI in software engineering 3 Digital twins 4 Evolutionary algorithms Interactive figures require JavaScript. Static diagrams, captions and source tables remain available; displayed demo values are illustrative unless labeled as publication data. Place 12 wind turbines on a square kilometre, each on one of 100 cells of 100 × 100 m. There are 1.05 · 10 15 ways to choose the cells, before any spacing rule — checking a million layouts per second would take 33 years. Yet any single layout can be scored in an instant: so much energy, so much loss in the wake of the neighbours. When you can rate every candidate but cannot list them all, you can let the candidates evolve . An evolutionary algorithm keeps a population of candidates. It rates each by its fitness , lets the better ones have children — mixing their parts ( crossover ) and changing them a little at random ( mutation ) — and lets the worse ones die out ( selection ). Generation by generation, the population drifts toward good solutions. In code, it is a loop of a few lines: population = [random_candidate() for _ in range(20)] for generation in range(60): scored = [(fitness(c), c) for c in population] parents = select(scored) # the better ones, more often kids = [mutate(crossover(a, b)) for a, b in pairs(parents)] population = survivors(scored, kids) + [random_candidate(), random_candidate()] best = max(population, key=fitness) This article explains that loop step by step, on an example you can take in at a glance: a landscape with two hills, where a candidate is a point and its fitness is the height there. First chapter: where evolutionary algorithms sit next to the machine learning and LLMs of part 2 . Second: what each step does — with figures that run real, replayable evolutions. Third: the family, evolution in software engineering, and two applications from my own work — the wind farm returns there, as the case study of my master’s thesis.

title: Where evolutionary algorithms sit
text: Evolutionary algorithms are older than deep learning and work quite differently. To place them, ask what a method needs — and what it gives back.

title: The AI map
text: “AI” covers methods that have little in common. Some get a formal model of the problem — rules, constraints — and search it: route planners, SAT and SMT solvers. Some get examples and learn a model from them: regression, deep networks, LLMs. And some get only a score : a way to rate any candidate, without knowing why one is better. These interfaces overlap: basic evolutionary optimization uses the third interface, while neuroevolution can train models. The standard AI textbook files them under search and optimisation, next to hill climbing and simulated annealing [1] , not under learning. The border to machine learning is open, though. Evolution can tune the settings of a model or even grow its network — and if you have used Optuna for hyperparameters, you may already have run an evolutionary algorithm: its CMA-ES and NSGA-II samplers are exactly that. Genetic, local, global: three words that mislead “Genetic” is a metaphor. Holland’s genetic algorithms [2] borrowed the words — chromosome, gene, crossover, mutation — not the biology. Eiben and Smith warn that reading evolution as optimisation is natural but “somewhat misleading” [3] : nature has no fixed goal. This article says evolutionary algorithm for the whole family and genetic algorithm for the variant with chromosomes and crossover. Local or global? The textbook calls these methods “local search” because they keep only current candidates, not the paths to them [1] . A population still explores many regions at once — it can climb several hills in parallel.

title: Sort AI methods by what you give them and what you get back.
text: Sort AI methods by what you give them and what you get back. Typical interfaces, not disjoint categories: the basic EA needs a scalar evaluator. Multiobjective and quality-diversity variants need richer information; neuroevolution can return reusable models. you give the methods you get a formal model rules, constraints → search and solvers planners, SAT/SMT, integer programs → an answer for this one problem training data learning objective → machine learning regression, deep networks, LLMs → part 2 → a reusable model for new inputs only a score a way to rate any candidate → search with a score hill climbing, simulated annealing, evolutionary algorithms → good candidates for this one problem Overlap: evolution can also tune or grow a model — neuroevolution, hyperparameter search.

title: Learning from data vs searching with a score
text: A neural network learns by gradient descent : a differentiable learning objective supplies gradients. Training may be supervised, self-supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement-based; external labels are not always needed. The basic single-objective evolutionary loop instead needs a scalar score for each candidate — which may itself come from data or from a slow simulation — and it gives back good candidates: a layout, a schedule, a test suite. This basic loop returns solutions for the present objective; neuroevolution can also evolve reusable models or policies. Extensions may need multiple objectives, constraints, behavioral descriptors or local component scores. Both use randomness on purpose. In part 2, the temperature decides how often a language model picks a less likely word. In an evolutionary algorithm, randomness enters twice: selection gives better candidates better odds , not certainty, and mutation makes random changes no parent had. The two worlds meet in a new way. In FunSearch [4] and AlphaEvolve [5] , building on the idea of evolution through large models [6] , the candidates are programs: an LLM reads a few good ones and writes a variant, an automatic evaluator scores it, the best are kept and varied again. The LLM replaces the hand-written mutation — the loop and the score stay exactly as described here. WORTH IT WHEN you can score a candidate but have no gradient, the space is huge or oddly shaped, and hundreds of evaluations are affordable. SOMETHING ELSE IS ENOUGH WHEN a reliable gradient method or an exact solver fits, or only a few dozen evaluations are affordable. The full list is in the summary. No Free Lunch Is there a best optimiser? No: under a uniform average over all objective functions on a finite search space, non-revisiting black-box optimizers have equivalent performance — Wolpert and Macready’s No Free Lunch theorems [7] . This does not assert equivalence on a structured real-world problem distribution. The advantage comes from what you build in: an encoding where good parts can be combined, operators that respect the constraints, a score that rewards the right thing. The rest of this article is about exactly these choices. And one family, the evolution strategies, is closer to gradient descent than it seems: “ES can be seen as computing a finite difference derivative estimate in a randomly chosen direction” [8] .

title: What each needs, what each gives.
section: Learning from data vs searching with a score
text: What each needs, what each gives. Gradient-based learning uses data and a differentiable objective; the basic single-objective evolutionary search uses a scalar score — which may itself come from a simulation — and yields good candidates. Switch the variation step: in FunSearch [4] and AlphaEvolve [5] an LLM writes the variants, while the loop and the evaluator stay classical. VARIATION:

title: How an evolutionary algorithm works
text: The design choices are representation → objective and constraints → selection and variation → survivor policy → budget and measurements. The running example: a square landscape, x and y each from 0 to 1, with two hills. A candidate is a point (x, y); its fitness is the height of the landscape there. One hill is broad and low (height 0.6), the other narrow and high (1.0) — the first is easy to find, the second easy to miss. A run starts with random points and evolves them.

title: The loop
text: One pass through the loop is a generation ; the candidates of a generation are the population ; one candidate is a chromosome , its parts are genes — here, the two numbers x and y. Each generation: let the better candidates become parents, make children by mixing and tweaking parents, score the children, and keep the best of old and new. Step through one real generation: These are the five steps of the general scheme in Eiben and Smith’s textbook [3] . Libraries name and split them differently: some pair the parents up in a step of their own, some first choose which children to mutate, some add random newcomers after the survivors are picked. In my library geneial , each of these steps is an exchangeable building block. The shape stays the same.

title: One generation of a genetic algorithm.
text: One generation of a genetic algorithm. 10 candidates on the two-hills landscape; a candidate is a point (x, y), its fitness the height there. Each row is one candidate, the bar its height; the map shows where they stand. The settings are the starter’s at the end of the article (tournaments of 3, 30 % of the children mutated, an elite of 2), with half the population and one newcomer. Data: a seeded run (seed 13)

title: Encoding: what a candidate is
text: The genotype is what the algorithm manipulates; the phenotype is what it means. In the running example the two coincide — two numbers, one point. In most problems they do not, and the encoding is the main design decision: it decides how big the search space is and which mutation and crossover make sense. The first population is random. When not every genotype is valid — two turbines on the same spot, a city visited twice — either the encoding rules it out, a repair step fixes it, or the score punishes it. The same holds in software engineering, where choosing what a candidate is is most of the work:

text: Three encodings, three sets of operators. The genotype (top line) is what the algorithm changes; what it means — and therefore which mutation and crossover make sense — depends on the problem. Our running example is the third. title: And in software engineering.
text: And in software engineering. Choosing what a candidate is — and how to score it — is the creative part; the loop is the same. Edit indices of the GenProg column are illustrative. EvoSuite [9] chromosome: a whole test suite test 1: Stack s = new Stack(); s.push(5); test 2: Stack s = new Stack(); s.pop(); minimise: uncovered branches, and how far the tests miss each one GenProg [10] chromosome: a patch: a list of edits Delete(12) Insert(40, 7) Replace(81, 44) maximise: tests passed. Caution: a patch that deletes the failing feature can pass too PerOpteryx [11] chromosome: an architecture: components → servers Frontend → server 1 Orders → server 1 Billing → server 2 server 2: 4 cores several objectives at once: response time, cost, reliability (NSGA-II)

title: Fitness: the score is the specification
text: In the basic loop, scalar fitness ranks candidates; the encoding, operators and constraints also encode problem knowledge. In the running example it is a formula — the height. In real problems it is often a chain of models or a test run, and one evaluation can take minutes or days. And the algorithm optimises exactly that score, not what you meant. GenProg evolves patches until a failing test passes; it fixed 55 of 105 bugs for about eight dollars each [10] . A later analysis found that most of these patches were not correct — many simply deleted the faulty functionality [12] . The tests were the fitness, and the tests did not forbid deleting. The score is the specification : evolution optimises exactly what you measure. Three practical points. Budget: the cost of a run is the number of evaluations. The starter at the end of this article evaluates 20 random candidates and then 18 new ones per generation (16 children and 2 newcomers) for 60 generations: 20 + 60 × 18 = 1,100 — at one minute each, about 18 hours. Evaluate in parallel and cache scores. Constraints: invalid candidates can be repaired, penalised in the score, or made impossible by the encoding. Direction: this article maximises; many libraries minimise — negate the score. The NASA antenna A good specification can make evolution beat engineers. For NASA’s Space Technology 5 mission, Lohn and colleagues evolved the shape of a small wire antenna. To survive manufacturing tolerances, every design was simulated several times with small random perturbations of its angles and wire radii — and its fitness was the worst of these runs [13] . The result looked like a bent paperclip, met the requirements, and flew on the mission in 2006 — the first evolved hardware in space [14] .

title: Selection: who gets to have children
text: Selection turns fitness into chances. The classic roulette wheel gives each candidate a slice proportional to its fitness [15] . It has a weakness you can try below: it depends on the absolute numbers. A tournament draws k candidates at random and takes the best — it only compares, and k is a single dial [16] . A softmax with a temperature sits in between, exactly like the token choice of a language model. How strongly the better candidates are preferred. Too little, and the search drifts; too much, and the population collapses onto the first good idea. Elitism copies the best candidates unchanged into the next generation, so the best score can never get worse. But selection should not only pick the best: weaker parents get a chance on purpose, because their differences are what lets the population leave a mediocre hill. Takeover time How fast does selection alone — without crossover and mutation — fill a population with copies of the best? Goldberg and Deb called this the takeover time and compared the common schemes: proportional selection is slow when the scores are close together, tournament and ranking selection take over in a number of generations that grows only with the logarithm of the population size [16] . Fast takeover is good for refining and bad for exploring.

title: Crossover: mixing two parents
text: The selected parents are paired up, and crossover builds a child from both: the hope is that good parts of two parents combine into something better than either. How depends entirely on the encoding. On the two hills, the child takes x from one parent and y from the other — a corner of the rectangle the parents span, as in the loop figure. Numbers in a fixed order can be cut and spliced. A tour cannot: The general rule: an operator has to produce valid candidates, or a repair step must fix them. Operators that know the problem usually beat generic ones — the wind-farm case in chapter 03 shows one. Building blocks, carefully Why should crossover work at all? Holland’s schema theorem [2] gives a lower bound for how often short, above-average patterns of genes — schemata — are expected to appear in the next generation. That much is a theorem, under its assumptions. The popular follow-up, the building-block hypothesis — that GAs work by assembling such good blocks into ever better solutions — is contested [3] . One thing is easy to check: the coordinate-swapping crossover used here reshuffles parental values; mutation and newcomers introduce new values. Arithmetic or intermediate recombination can also create new numeric values.

Right: on a permutation, cutting and splicing repeats and drops cities; order crossover keeps a slice of one parent and the order of the other. City positions illustrative, lengths computed. The order means something, so a cut makes sense: children inherit whole stretches. A TOUR: ORDER CROSSOVER

title: Mutation: three knobs
text: Mutation changes a candidate randomly, with the scale and probability chosen for the representation. In this example, Gaussian mutation and random newcomers introduce new values; arithmetic crossover could do so too. Mutation can also spoil a good child. “Mutation rate” sounds like one setting; in fact there are three: Small steps refine, big steps explore; without mutation, newcomers or other novelty-producing operators, this coordinate-swapping search cannot introduce new coordinate values. Mutation is also the slot that the LLMs from chapter 01 fill: in FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, the “mutation” is a language model rewriting a program. Step sizes that tune themselves Choosing the step size by hand is tedious, so evolution strategies let it adapt. Rechenberg’s 1/5 success rule : if more than a fifth of the mutations improve, take bigger steps; if fewer, smaller ones [18] . Self-adaptation puts the step size into the genome, so that it evolves along. CMA-ES goes furthest: it learns a whole covariance matrix — which directions are promising and how they correlate — from the path the search has taken [19] .

title: Three knobs, not one.
text: Three knobs, not one. Twenty copies of one child go through mutation. mutpb : the chance that a child is mutated at all; indpb : the chance per number (below 1, some mutants move only sideways or only up and down); sigma : the step size — the circle has radius σ, and before boundary clamping, 1 − exp(−1/2) ≈ 39.35 % of isotropic Gaussian steps lie inside it when both coordinates mutate. Coordinates are clamped to [0, 1]. Filled: higher than the child, hollow: lower. The names are those of DEAP; the starter at the end mutates exactly one of the two numbers. Mutants are drawn live. THE CHILD: sigma step size σ indpb chance per number mutpb chance per child

title: Survivors, newcomers and diversity
text: After the children are scored, the survivors are selected. The starter keeps its elite and replaces everybody else with the children; evolution strategies name the alternatives — (μ + λ) picks the survivors from parents and children together, (μ, λ) from the children only [18] . A few random newcomers are added after that choice: they are almost always below average and would not survive a fair comparison. Why bother? Because a population converges when it loses its diversity — when most candidates become alike. If that happens too early, it has converged on the wrong hill. Searching new regions vs refining near what is known to be good. Every knob of the loop moves the balance between the two [3] . Watch both on the two hills — a whole run, generation by generation: Three ways to read such charts — they are worth logging in any real run. Diversity flat early: too much pressure. The mean no better than random: too many newcomers, the run has become random search. And always compare against random search with the same number of evaluations: here it found the right hill in all 10 runs — but reached its top in only 2 of them, the balanced setting in 6. A good evolutionary algorithm explores and refines. Keeping diversity on purpose Random newcomers are only one way to keep diversity. Fitness sharing divides the score of candidates that crowd the same spot, so that a crowded hill becomes less attractive; crowding lets a child replace the parent it resembles most, so that niches survive [3] . Novelty search goes all the way and rewards being different instead of being good — and still finds good solutions on deceptive problems [20] . Novelty archives record behavioral novelty; by contrast, quality-diversity methods such as MAP-Elites keep a high-quality candidate per behavior niche (chapter 03).

Top chart: best, mean and worst fitness; the band between best and worst is the fitness gap . Bottom: diversity (mean distance to the centre of the population) — this mean radial distance can hide multiple clusters. Zero means collapsed positions, not proof of an optimum. title: When to stop
text: In most real problems you do not know the best possible score — on the two hills we do, in a wind farm nobody does. So runs stop after a budget: a number of generations, of evaluations, or of seconds; or when the best has not improved for a while; or when a target is reached. Criteria can be combined. The hybrid car in chapter 03 stops after exactly 100 generations, because the controller must answer in fixed time [NWN+15] . Evolutionary algorithms are anytime algorithms: you can stop them whenever you like and take the best so far — and most of the gain usually comes early, as the charts above show.

title: Evolutionary algorithms in practice
text: The family beyond the genetic algorithm, evolution in software engineering, two problems from my own work, and how to start.

title: The family
text: “Evolutionary algorithm” is a family name. Its members differ mainly in two choices: what a candidate is — which decides how it can be varied — and what you want back — which decides what survives. Genetic algorithms (GA): strings of genes, crossover as the main operator [15] — the dialect of this article. Evolution strategies (ES) and CMA-ES : real-valued vectors, mutation with adapting step sizes. The default for continuous parameters. Differential evolution (DE): mutates by adding the difference of two other candidates, then crosses with the parent and keeps the better of the two. Genetic programming (GP): candidates are programs — the basis of GenProg and genetic improvement. NSGA-II : several objectives at once; seeks an approximation to a non-dominated set of trade-offs instead of one best. In model-driven engineering, PerOpteryx uses it to optimise software architecture models for performance, reliability and cost — see part 1 for models. MAP-Elites stores high-quality candidates per behavioral niche; novelty search rewards behavioral difference, with archives serving a different purpose. AlphaEvolve uses related archive-based program search. NEAT and neuroevolution: evolve neural networks, topology included. Evolution at scale Evolution strategies also scale like few other methods. Because each candidate is scored independently and only scores need to be exchanged, Salimans and colleagues ran ES on 1,440 workers and taught a simulated humanoid to walk “in under 10 minutes” — a competitive alternative to reinforcement learning with gradients [8] . David Ha’s visual guide shows several of these strategies side by side on 2-D landscapes like our two hills [25] .

title: Evolution in software engineering
text: In 2001, Harman and Jones proposed to treat software-engineering problems the same way: find a representation for a candidate and a fitness to score it, and let a search do the rest — search-based software engineering [26] . You have met GenProg in chapter 02; three more examples show how far this goes. Test generation. EvoSuite evolves whole test suites for Java classes. A test with x = 5 misses if (x >= 10) by 5; one with x = 9 misses it by only 1. EvoSuite scores that gap, so the search can feel its way toward the branch instead of seeing only “covered / not covered” [9] . Faster programs. Genetic improvement evolves edits to existing code: it made a 50,000-line bioinformatics tool 70 times faster on average on its benchmark [27] . App testing at scale. Sapienz evolves sequences of user actions and found 558 unknown crashes in the top 1,000 Android apps [28] .

title: Case: wind-farm layout
text: The problem of the hook, for real: Horns Rev 1 in the Danish North Sea, 80 Vestas V80 turbines on 3.8 × 5 km, wind data of eight years, each layout rated by annual energy production, net present value and internal rate of return. Genetic algorithms are a classic tool for placing wind turbines [29] ; my master’s thesis asked a narrower question — how to encode the positions — and compared operators for it [Net17] . Three things make the problem harder than the two hills. The first is the score: behind every turbine the air is slower. The second is the encoding. Before the real wind model, the thesis tested its operators on toy scores such as “better toward the north-east” on a 1 km site with 12 turbines, at least 240 m apart. A position can be a free floating-point pair or a cell of an n × n grid — and the grid is a design decision with consequences: The lesson that carries over to any problem: as a practical heuristic, avoid precision that adds cost without measurable improvement under the tested objective and budget. How big is the search space, honestly? The textbook encoding for wind farms is one bit per cell: 1 = a turbine stands here [29] . It is intuitive and fine for coarse grids. But for a fine one the arithmetic explodes: with 10,000 cells per axis, a single chromosome has 10 8 bits, and a population of 1000 requires 12.5 GB (about 11.64 GiB) for packed genes alone: 12.5 MB per candidate. A byte per cell instead requires 100 GB before container overhead. A list of coordinates stays the same size however fine the grid. And a fun fact on precision: two neighbouring 64-bit floating-point numbers near 1000 m are about 10 −13 m apart — far below the size of an atom. No wind model resolves that. The third is crossover. A layout is a set of positions, not a sequence: which turbine is “gene 3”? The thesis built a problem-aware operator for it: One-Step crossover does not create a single new position; it only recombines. Problem-aware operators like this one beat the generic ones in the thesis — but only because the simulation reports a score for every turbine. If your evaluator returns one number per candidate, there is nothing to rank by. The general rule: if your evaluator can give partial scores, use them. On the real site, finally, both encodings ran with their recommended setups: The thesis concludes that grid genes were much more efficient and gave better results in all its test cases. Read with the caveat in the caption, the lesson is the one from above: match the resolution of the genes to the resolution of the score, and do not pay for precision nobody can see.

With a west wind, every turbine slows the air behind it: in the middle row the second turbine keeps 37 %, the third 30 %, and even 1000 m downstream a wake still costs 22 %. Move one turbine and other turbines’ numbers change — the genes are not independent. title: Case: energy management in a hybrid car
text: The 2015 paper studies a parallel hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV in that paper): combustion and electric motors coupled on a common drive axis. The simulation updates torque distribution every 20 ms; the optimized split may be held for up to one second before recalculation. The optimization looks ahead 20 seconds. These are simulation results, not road trials. In the DFG project OASys at RWTH’s Theory of Hybrid Systems group, we built a controller around a genetic algorithm [NWN+15] ; geneial started as its framework. The weights are the specification, as with GenProg in chapter 02: telling the GA to care only about fuel gave a worse fuel result than adding “keep the battery near its target” — one possible explanation, not causally tested in the paper, is that the battery term adds foresight beyond the 20-second window. With the best weighting, the GA used 1.8 % less fuel in the simulated NEDC benchmark than the best compared published reference strategy (Table 2 versus Table 1). And smooth driving — the engine should not switch on and off every second — competes with fuel: Why a GA inside a controller? Why a GA inside a control loop, where every step has a deadline? Because it is an anytime algorithm with a fixed budget: the paper reports 50 candidates and 100 generations as real-time-capable in its benchmark, allowing a split to be held for up to one second. This does not establish a 20 ms optimization deadline on a production ECU. Because its population carries over from step to step — shifted by one gene, it is already a good guess for the next decision. And because the fitness can be any mix of goals, including ones that are hard to put into a formula for a classical controller. A larger population starts and ends higher, but costs time; 50 was the compromise for real time.

title: Try it: settings and libraries
text: The whole algorithm of the convergence figure, in plain Python without any library — the “balanced” setting on the two hills. Copy it, run it, then change one knob at a time: import math, random def fitness(g): # two hills: broad and low, narrow and high x, y = g low = 0.6 * math.exp(-((x - 0.25)**2 + (y - 0.30)**2) / 0.08) high = 1.0 * math.exp(-((x - 0.80)**2 + (y - 0.75)**2) / 0.006) return max(low, high) def new(): # initialisation: a random candidate return [random.random(), random.random()] def run(seed, size=20, gens=60, elite=2, newcomers=2, k=3, p_mut=0.3, step=0.05): random.seed(seed) evals = 0 def score(cands): # evaluate each candidate once nonlocal evals evals += len(cands) return [(fitness(g), g) for g in cands] pop = sorted(score([new() for _ in range(size)]), reverse=True) for gen in range(gens): # stop: a fixed budget of generations def pick(): # tournament selection return max(random.sample(pop, k))[1] kids = [] for _ in range(size - elite - newcomers): a, b = pick(), pick() # uniform crossover: each gene from one of the two parents child = [random.choice(p) for p in zip(a, b)] if random.random() < p_mut: # mutate some children i = random.randrange(2) child[i] = min(1, max(0, child[i] + random.gauss(0, step))) kids.append(child) kids += [new() for _ in range(newcomers)] # random newcomers # elitism + replacement: the best survive, the rest is replaced pop = sorted(pop[:elite] + score(kids), reverse=True) return pop[0], evals for seed in range(1, 11): (f, best), evals = run(seed) print(seed, [round(v, 2) for v in best], round(f, 3), evals) WHAT YOU WILL SEE Seeds 4, 5 and 7 end on the low hill with fitness 0.600; seeds 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9 and 10 reach the high one (≥ 0.99). Every run costs 1,100 evaluations. Three out of ten on the wrong hill — that is why you run seeds. Try newcomers=0 , k=8 or p_mut=0 and count again. SENSIBLE FIRST SETTINGS Start from the starter’s defaults — 20 candidates, tournaments of 3, 30 % of the children mutated with a step of 5 % of the range, an elite of 2, 2 newcomers, 60 generations — or from your library’s defaults. Scale the population with the size of the problem. Then start with at least ten seeds, log best, mean and diversity, and compare with random search at the same evaluation budget. For research claims, also report uncertainty, evaluation and wall-clock budgets, stopping criteria, feasibility and hardware; tune configurations on separate instances. Who tunes the tuner? Every setting is itself a parameter of the search, and choosing them is an optimisation problem of its own — GA configurations are often tuned with GAs. The field distinguishes parameter tuning , fixing the settings before a run, from parameter control , changing them during the run, as self-adapting step sizes do [3] . For real problems, use a library; they differ in what they make easy, and they name the knobs differently: Many libraries fold the loop into three verbs: ask for new candidates (select, recombine, mutate), evaluate them yourself, tell the algorithm the scores (it decides who survives). Here is that ask–tell loop with CMA-ES for two real numbers (adapted from the cmaes README): import numpy as np from cmaes import CMA def quadratic(x1, x2): return (x1 - 3) ** 2 + (10 * (x2 + 2)) ** 2 optimizer = CMA(mean=np.zeros(2), sigma=1.3) for generation in range(50): solutions = [] for _ in range(optimizer.population_size): x = optimizer.ask() # propose solutions.append((x, quadratic(x[0], x[1]))) # score optimizer.tell(solutions) # keep the better, adapt To watch evolution without writing code, try Genetic Cars 2 ↗ , where a GA breeds two-wheeled cars and lets you change the mutation rate and the elite while they drive. The library behind my thesis, geneial , is open source (C++11, MIT) [31] but no longer maintained. And if your system already has a digital twin , an optimiser like these can become one of its services.

title: In short
text: One loop with exchangeable parts: select parents, recombine and mutate, evaluate, select survivors, repeat. You write the encoding and the score; libraries supply the rest. The basic loop needs a scalar evaluator; extensions may need more information. The price is evaluations: population × generations, each possibly a slow simulation. The encoding is the main design decision. It decides which operators make sense and how big the space is; choose precision that justifies its evaluation cost under the tested objective and budget. The score is the specification. Evolution optimises exactly what you measure — patches that delete features, a fuel-only controller that uses more fuel. Selection pressure works against diversity. Every knob moves the balance between exploring and exploiting; a run that loses its diversity has converged, right or wrong. Randomness is a tool, so measure it: run several seeds, log best, mean and diversity, and compare with random search. WORTH IT WHEN you can score a candidate, but there is no gradient the space is huge, discrete or mixed, with many local optima several objectives pull against each other hundreds to thousands of evaluations are affordable, and “very good” is good enough SOMETHING ELSE IS ENOUGH WHEN a gradient method efficiently handles the objective and constraints an exact solver fits the problem — SAT, SMT, integer programming (see SMT-RAT ) only a few dozen evaluations are affordable you need a guarantee of optimality

title: ESACA
text: since 2026 AI coding agents are fast — and they read code, run commands and send data wherever they like. ESACA lets regulated organisations use them anyway: inside their own data centre, under their own rules. title: Agents, code, secrets and models stay inside the organisation’s perimeter.
text: Agents, code, secrets and models stay inside the organisation’s perimeter. The agent works in a sandbox and only ever sees placeholder credentials; a second container decides — and logs — what may leave.

title: The problem
text: Banks, utilities, public authorities and defence suppliers face the same dilemma. Agentic coding promises large productivity gains, but a cloud-based agent can send source code and secrets to a foreign provider, delete data or pull in a malicious extension — and it ties the organisation to one vendor’s model, prices and roadmap. Banning the tools only pushes teams into shadow IT, where nobody measures what the agents actually deliver.

title: The idea
text: ESACA — the European Sovereign Agentic Coding Appliance — is a standardised system that brings coding agents into the organisation’s own perimeter: on-premises or fully air-gapped, with no data egress, no external API calls and no hidden telemetry. It is model-independent and favours sovereign models running on the customer’s own hardware. ESACA is an initiative of mgm technology partners and Fsas Technologies, a Fujitsu company. In the terms of my article on AI-driven software engineering , it is a harness for coding agents.

title: The building blocks
text: Sandbox — the agent and the project run in one container, all outbound traffic goes through a second one. Access is deny-by-default, the agent only sees placeholder credentials, real secrets are injected on the way out, every decision is logged. Configuration — one versionable file describes the whole environment: access rules, agents, skills, plugins, tools and versions. Hub — proven configurations are shared and reused across projects. Benchmark — measures the complete system (agent + model + hardware) on the organisation’s own repositories, keeping hard metrics such as builds and tests apart from LLM-as-judge scores. Workbench — a guided path from ticket to plan to agents in isolated workspaces, ending in a mandatory human review before the normal merge process.

title: Who it is for
text: Critical infrastructure and utilities, the public sector, and regulated industries such as defence, legal and healthcare — organisations that work under NIS-2, BaFin, ISO 27001 and GDPR. The adoption path goes step by step, from assistants to agents, multi-agent workflows and finally AI-native development, with people staying in the decision seat.
