title: One of the 45 cases: the natural-language description (left) and the reviewed reference model (right).
text: One of the 45 cases: the natural-language description (left) and the reviewed reference model (right). Case University , contributed by the Business Informatics Group, TU Wien — CC BY 4.0. open the case ↗ description · University A university consists of several faculties, which are made up of various institutes. Each faculty and institute has a name. The address of each institute is known. Each faculty is headed by a dean, who is an employee of the university. The total number of employees is known. Employees have a social security number, a name, and an email address. A distinction is made between research and administrative staff. Research assistants (RA) are assigned to at least one institute. The field of research of each RA is known. In addition, RAs can be involved in projects for a certain number of hours, whereby the name, start and end dates of the projects are known. Some RAs teach courses. In this case, they are referred to as lecturers. Courses have a unique number (ID), a name and a weekly duration in hours.

title: The problem
text: The large existing UML collections were built by crawling GitHub and online modelling platforms. They are full of syntactically broken, semantically wrong, duplicate and placeholder models — and almost none of them come with the text that says what the model is supposed to represent. Without that text you cannot tell whether a model is right, so they are weak as exercises and weak as benchmarks. The text-to-UML datasets built for LLMs, on the other hand, contain at most a dozen models or no reference solutions at all.

title: The dataset
text: The Golden UML Model Set goes the other way: fewer models, all of them reviewed. It starts with 45 cases from modelling courses and exams at RWTH Aachen, TU Wien, KU Leuven and McGill, plus a database textbook — exercises refined over years of student feedback. Every case pairs a requirements text with a class diagram in PlantUML; many add extra material such as alternative or deliberately wrong solutions with explanations. Cases are labelled by domain, from sales and logistics to healthcare and education. 45 cases 5 sources 28 with inheritance 17 with association classes

title: Growing it together
text: Anyone can contribute a case through a web form or a GitHub pull request. At least one reviewer checks it against a checklist — completeness and duplicates, metadata, clarity of the description, UML syntax, and whether the model actually matches the text. Approved cases appear immediately on a searchable web platform with filters for domain, size and modelling constructs; versioned snapshots go to Zenodo and Hugging Face so that research can cite an exact release.

title: What it is for
text: Teaching — a shared pool of modelling exercises with solutions, and variants of a case to train students in judging solutions against requirements. LLM evaluation — generative AI almost always produces some model; the question is its quality. Reviewed reference solutions make it possible to compare generated models semantically against a ground truth. Publications · 1 VNG+25 Toward a Community-Curated Golden Dataset of UML Models C. title: Answers come from the lecture’s own material, not from the model’s general knowledge — and the questions…
text: Answers come from the lecture’s own material, not from the model’s general knowledge — and the questions students ask flow back to the lecturer.

title: The problem
text: General-purpose chatbots answer lecture questions with general knowledge: plausible, but often at the wrong level, with different notation than the course, and sometimes simply wrong. Lecturers, meanwhile, only find out what students did not understand when they grade the exam.

title: How it works
text: SE-Chatty is fed with the lecture’s own material — scripts, books, slides and videos. For every question it first retrieves the relevant passages and then lets the language model answer on that basis ( retrieval-augmented generation ). The answers therefore follow the course: its terms, its examples, its depth.

title: For students and lecturers
text: Students ask questions at any time and prepare for the exam with generated questionnaires. Lecturers see which parts of the material are understood — and which aren’t — while the course is still running.

title: The display of a thesis, from the doctoral office to the dean’s office — what used to be paper copies in a…
text: The display of a thesis, from the doctoral office to the dean’s office — what used to be paper copies in a room is now a web application.

title: The problem
text: At a German faculty, a dissertation or habilitation is not just accepted by the reviewers: for a fixed period, every professor of the faculty may read the thesis and the reviews and raise concerns before the faculty decides. Traditionally that meant paper copies in the dean’s office — professors had to come by during opening hours to read them.

title: How it works
text: The doctoral office creates a display for each thesis: candidate, title, subject group, reviewers and examiners, the documents as PDFs — thesis, summary, bibliography, reviews — and the display period. Professors are notified by e-mail, either immediately or in a weekly digest, filtered by the subject groups they care about. During the period they read everything online and can send a comment — praise, criticism or a neutral note — directly to the dean’s office. Invitations to the defence go out from the same application.

title: Model-driven
text: ePHA is a small application by design, and that is exactly where model-driven development pays off: the domain — theses, documents, reviewers, displays, comments, notification settings — is described as a class diagram, and the application is generated from it with the MontiGem tool chain. The result runs in production for the Faculty of Mathematics, Computer Science and Natural Sciences.

title: The problem

title: The system
text: Every tool gets a small, heat- and water-resistant Bluetooth tag; every vehicle a tracking module that knows which tools are on board and reports their positions via GPS to a central server. If a tool is missing when the van is about to leave, the driver is reminded; if one moves when it shouldn’t, the owner is alerted. A web application shows everything on desktops, phones and a tablet in the vehicle: search by vehicle, storage place, tool type or name, photo tiles of the tools, and a live map of where each one was last seen.

title: Generated, not hand-written
text: The web application was largely generated with our MontiGem framework from UML models of the data, the user interface and standard behaviour. That made fast iterations possible, and the models became a shared language between Ford’s marketing experts, engineers, designers and the craftspeople. Two extensions grew out of the project and went back into the generator: multi-language support (German for the craftspeople, English for Ford’s managers) with an in-app translation editor, and a driving-safe tablet UI that shows less information while the vehicle is moving, based on its measured acceleration.

title: Field test
text: Three trade companies of different sizes around Cologne — construction and renovation, plumbing, gardening and landscaping — used the system for about eleven months. The application was improved continuously from their feedback and from usage data. text: A page nobody drew: the detail view of a pitch configuration, generated by CD2GUI straight from the class diagram (2021).

title: The problem
text: In wind-turbine engineering many disciplines work on the same machine: mechanics, electrics, control, simulation. Their parameters depend on each other, and a value changed in one place has to reach every other. In practice it travelled as e-mail attachments and files on individual laptops — outdated values crept in, and past simulation results were hard to find again. Agile and plan-driven development had to come together on one reliable data basis.

title: The cockpit
text: The result is a web cockpit — an engineering digital twin “as designed” — where engineers look up, edit, version and release parameters, CAD files and simulation results. A change history and archive, a release lifecycle (draft → review → released → outdated) with a check that released objects only point to released objects, and a diff view keep every value traceable. A Python library connects the engineering tools themselves — Rhino, Ansys, SpaceClaim — so they read and write the data through the API instead of local files.

title: Generated from one class diagram

title: MontiGem
text: 2018 — 2024 Describe the data and the pages in small, precise models — and get a complete web application: database, Java back end, API and Angular front end. MontiGem is the generator behind most of my projects . Role Co-creator Based on MontiCore Used in 5 domains Output Java · TypeScript · HTML MontiCore ↗ Background: Part 1 · Model-Driven Software Engineering → Background: Part 2 · AI-Driven Software Engineering →

title: From models to a running application.
text: From models to a running application. Each model language has a parser generated by MontiCore; the syntax trees are transformed and printed by FreeMarker templates into an Angular front end and a Java back end. CD2GUI (dashed) can derive the GUI models from the class diagram. Handwritten code lives in separate folders and extends the generated classes (TOP mechanism), so everything can be regenerated at any time. After [Net24] , Fig. 7.1.

title: The idea
text: Business information systems look different on the surface but are built from the same parts again and again: data classes, persistence, validation, an API, lists, forms and detail pages. Writing these by hand is slow, repetitive and error-prone — and every change to the domain ripples through all layers. MontiGem (MontiCore-based Ge nerator for E nterprise M anagement) generates them instead, from a class diagram for the data, GUI models for the pages and optional OCL constraints for validation.

title: How it works
text: The generator follows the classic compiler pipeline (figure above). MontiCore-generated parsers turn each model into a syntax tree; model-to-model transformations reshape it into the structure of the target code; FreeMarker templates print it as Java, TypeScript and HTML. For every domain class this yields a JPA data class, a DAO, a builder, a validator, DTOs and the commands of the API — on the server and, identically, on the client. Each GUI model becomes an Angular page. The generic parts — runtime components, styling, authentication with Apache Shiro — come from a hand-written runtime environment that is never regenerated.

title: Generated and handwritten
text: No generator covers everything, so the interesting question is how hand-written code fits in. MontiGem uses the TOP mechanism : if a developer writes a class with the name of a generated one, the generator emits its version as …TOP instead, and the hand-written class extends it. Generated and hand-written code live in separate folders; the whole application can be regenerated at any time without losing a single line. // generated, because Account.java exists in the handwritten folder public class AccountTOP { … } // handwritten — survives every regeneration public class Account extends AccountTOP { @Override public BigDecimal getBalance() { … } }

title: Five domains
text: MontiGem grew inside MaCoCo and was later extracted into a framework of its own — I built its first version together with Simon Varga and Kai Adam. It has since been used in five domains, each of which pushed new features back into the generator: MaCoCo — financial, staff and project management for university chairs; OCL validation. Ford — IoT tool tracking; multi-language UIs and a driving-safe tablet view. Agile Data Development — wind-turbine engineering; CD2GUI generates the pages from the class diagram. Energy management of buildings, and InviDas — comparing the privacy policies of wearables. In [Net24] , MontiGem is the last link of a chain: an LLM turns a natural-language description into a class diagram, CD2GUI derives the GUI models, and MontiGem generates the application — from text to a running web app. How that works . title: geneial
text: 2012 — 2017 Some problems are too big to solve exactly — so you let solutions evolve . geneial is a C++ library for genetic algorithms in which every step of evolution is an exchangeable building block. Type C++11 library License MIT Authors Wolters · Netz · Nellen github ↗ OASys ↗ Background: Part 4 · Evolutionary Algorithms →

title: One generation of an evolutionary algorithm — every box is an exchangeable operator in geneial.
text: One generation of an evolutionary algorithm — every box is an exchangeable operator in geneial. From [Net17] .

title: The idea
text: A genetic algorithm imitates evolution. A population of candidate solutions — chromosomes — is rated by a fitness function; the best are selected, paired, recombined and randomly mutated, and the next generation is formed from the offspring, an elite of the old generation and a few fresh random candidates. Repeated over many generations, the population drifts towards good solutions, even for problems that cannot be solved exactly in reasonable time.

title: Where it comes from
text: geneial was created at RWTH’s Theory of Hybrid Systems group in the context of the DFG project OASys — online algorithms for the optimal control of hybrid propulsion systems. There it served as the framework for a genetic-algorithm-based control strategy for the energy management of parallel hybrid vehicles: when should the combustion engine run, when the electric motor?

title: The library
text: geneial is a template-based C++11 library. Each stage of the loop in the figure above — stopping criteria, selection, coupling, crossover, choosing, mutation, replacement — is an operator with its own builder, so users plug in their own chromosome types, operators and fitness functions. Fitness evaluation can run multi-threaded, and observers and bookkeepers make runs analysable. The project comes with a CMake build, Boost unit tests, benchmarks, Doxygen documentation and CI. A minimal run: auto evaluator = std::make_shared<DemoChromosomeEvaluator>(); ContinousMultiValueChromosomeFactory<int,double>::Builder factoryBuilder(evaluator); factoryBuilder.getSettings().setNum(20); factoryBuilder.getSettings().setRandomMin(20); factoryBuilder.getSettings().setRandomMax(130); auto algorithm = SteadyStateAlgorithm<double>::Builder() .setChromosomeFactory(factoryBuilder.create()).create(); algorithm->getPopulationSettings().setMaxChromosomes(100); algorithm->solve(); std::cout << *algorithm->getHighestFitnessChromosome() << std::endl;

title: Wind farms
text: Later I used geneial for a different problem [Net17] : placing the turbines of an offshore wind farm, rated by annual energy production, net present value and internal rate of return on the Horns Rev test cases. The question was whether turbine positions should be free continuous coordinates or points on a grid. The answer was clear: as long as the grid is fine enough, discretised gene parameters converge faster and reach better results in every test case. title: SMT-RAT
text: 2015 Does a set of polynomial inequalities over the real numbers have a solution? SMT-RAT answers questions like this from modules that can be combined into a solver — I worked on the one that narrows the search space with interval arithmetic. Type SMT solver toolbox · C++ Group Theory of Hybrid Systems, RWTH My part ICP module documentation ↗ github ↗ Background: Part 4 · Evolutionary Algorithms →

title: The dependency problem.
text: The dependency problem. Interval arithmetic treats every occurrence of x as an independent value from [0, 1], so x² − x comes out as [−1, 1] — eight times wider than the true range. Rewritten as a Horner scheme, x appears less often and the result tightens to [−1, 0]. Tighter intervals let ICP cut away more of the search space in each step.

title: The problem
text: Many questions in verification and engineering boil down to one: is there an assignment of real numbers that satisfies a Boolean combination of polynomial constraints? Can this hybrid system reach an unsafe state, does this rewrite system terminate, does this inequality hold? Such formulas of non-linear real arithmetic are decidable, but the complete methods are expensive — at least exponential in the worst case.

title: SMT-RAT
text: SMT solvers combine a fast SAT solver for the Boolean structure with theory solvers for the arithmetic. SMT-RAT (Satisfiability-Modulo-Theories Real Algebra Toolbox), developed at RWTH’s Theory of Hybrid Systems group, makes the theory part modular: each method — simplex, virtual substitution, interval constraint propagation, cylindrical algebraic decomposition and more — is a module, and a strategy chains modules into a solver. Cheap, incomplete methods go first and hand a smaller problem to the expensive, complete ones. The toolbox is open source, reads SMT-LIB 2 and builds on the CArL library for polynomials.

title: Interval constraint propagation
text: Interval constraint propagation (ICP) works on boxes of intervals, one per variable. It uses each constraint to cut away parts of the box that cannot contain a solution — contraction — until the box is empty (unsatisfiable) or small enough to hand on. Its weak spot is interval arithmetic itself: it does not know that two occurrences of x are the same number. That dependency problem makes results wider than necessary (figure above), so ICP contracts less and needs more iterations.

title: My contribution
text: I improved SMT-RAT’s ICP module in two ways [Net15] . First, a new contraction method — interval propagation through the constraint — in addition to the existing Newton-based contraction. Second, a data structure for multivariate Horner schemes : polynomials are rewritten in nested form, which needs fewer operations and repeats variables less often, so the intervals stay tighter. Two heuristics choose the variable to factor out next — one fast, one aimed at the smallest over-approximation — and a simplification step compresses the result. Evaluated on the standard SMT-LIB benchmark sets, the propagation clearly paid off: on keymaera (hybrid-systems verification) more instances were solved with fewer timeouts in little more than half the time, and on hong nearly twice as many test cases could be solved in the same time frame. The Horner schemes did make ICP more precise — up to 46 % fewer contractions on some instances — but building them cost more time than the tighter intervals saved. An honest result that pointed to the next steps: choosing the heuristic per input, and evaluating polynomials from the perspective of a single variable.
